new_statements.quote: Marri Amu is not clearly distinct, and from the data available it appears that Marri Tjevin and Marri Amu are largely a shared linguistic code [...] we have drawn on sources labelled both 'Tjevin' and 'Amu'. [...] We have not observed contrastive stress in Marri Tjevin, nor have we observed canonical lexical stress effects in terms of vowel duration and vowel quality (cf. Mansfield, forthcoming). However, the accentual alignment system does reflect word structure [...] Pitch accents occur at the beginning of the word in simple words such as nouns, but in complex verbs the pitch accent is instead anchored to the word-medial coverb. [...] The tonic is therefore the first syllable of simple words, the first syllable of a disyllabic coverb in complex verbs, or the syllable preceding a monosyllabic coverb.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive lexical stress and no canonical stress correlates (vowel duration/quality) observed. Prosodic prominence is a pitch accent whose position is predictable from word structure: on the first syllable of simple words (nouns, with or without a classifier proclitic, which is never prominent), and in complex verbs on the coverb (its first syllable if disyllabic; the syllable before it if monosyllabic), i.e. a word-initial accent in simple words and a morphologically anchored accent in verbs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned for Marri Tjevin/Marri Amu. (Second-hand only: Mansfield 2022 sec. 5.4 says related Western Daly languages are 'described as having initial primary stress for all word types' with secondary stress on the coverb, citing Green 1989 for Marrithiyel.)
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 12: the coverb-anchored pattern is 'the dominant alignment pattern', but 'some apparent variation in accentual alignment in complex verbs' was observed; 'Comprehensive analysis of Brinkin accentual placement will require much more extensive research.' The pitch peak often falls at the boundary between first and second syllables ('late rise'), interpreted as anchored to the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (pitch accent alignment measured on nouns and complex verbs in elicited sentences and narratives, Mansfield field recordings 2012-2017 plus Kofod 1986 tapes); phrasal prosody explicitly not analysed. The authors state at the outset that no contrastive word stress was observed, so 'stress' in the catalog sense is absent and the statement concerns accent placement.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes stress under the name Marri Ammu. The quoted statement is from Mansfield & Green 2021, whose object is labelled 'Marri Tjevin' (Maridjabin, mari1421, ISO zmj) but which explicitly pools data labelled 'Tjevin' and 'Amu' (Kofod 1986 tapes recorded in Marrijebin and Marriamo) and states that Marri Tjevin and Marri Amu 'are largely a shared linguistic code'. Tryon 1974 (p. 101) and Ford in Marett, Barwick & Ford 2013 (p. 83) independently say the two have identical phonologies; the Daly Languages site notes Aboriginal experts report 'minor phonological differences'. Glottolog treats Marri Ammu (marr1256), Maridjabin (mari1421), Maridan (mari1422) and Marrithiyel (mari1424) as separate languages, whereas Green 1989 treats all four as dialects of Marrithiyel. If the catalog adopts this statement for marr1256 it duplicates the mari1421 entry; the Marrithiyel stem-initial stress rule (Green 1989 sec. 2.1.3) is NOT Marri Ammu data.

sources.citation: Bicevskis, Katie. 2023. A grammar of Marri Ngarr. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne (bibliography and sec. 1.3).
sources.note: Marri Ngarr (a different Western Daly language; 70% cognates with Marri Amu per Tryon 1974) has stem-initial primary stress in nominals and stress on the lexical stem in bipartite verbs -- Marri Ngarr data, not Marri Ammu. Consulted for its bibliography: Ford, Lysbeth Julie 2010a. Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin Learner's Guide. Batchelor Institute Press; Long et al. 2016 Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin plants and animals.

sources.note: Zero descriptive references; endangerment comment quotes Brown 1999 ('only a handful of elderly Marriammu people are strong speakers').

sources.citation: Green, Ian. 1989. Marrithiyel: a language of the Daly River region of Australia's Northern Territory. PhD thesis, ANU. sec. 1.4 'Dialects and Surrounding Languages' pp. 8-9; sec. 2.1.3 'Word Stress' pp. 33-39.
sources.note: sec. 1.4: Marri Ammu ('plains language') is one of three dialects Marrithiyel speakers call 'one language'; Green did no fieldwork on it ('the remaining Marri Ammu were based at Port Keats'); informants 'aware of no similar phonological differences with the western dialects, Marrisjabin and Marri Ammu'. sec. 2.1.3 p. 34 (MARRITHIYEL data only): 'Primary stress is normally assigned to the first syllable of a stem, and secondary stress to the second syllable thereafter'; class prefixes do not attract stress; reduplicated roots take two primary stresses. Not Marri Ammu data.

sources.citation: Mansfield, John. 2022. Word prominence in polysynthetic Australian languages: Bininj Gun-wok, Ngalakgan and Murrinhpatha. PsyArXiv preprint doi:10.31234/osf.io/9wexr (published 2023 in Bogomolets & van der Hulst eds, Word Prominence in Languages with Complex Morphologies, OUP). sec. 5.4 'Other Daly languages', p. 34.
sources.note: Second-hand survey line: Western Daly languages 'Marrithiyel, Marri Ngarr and Emmi (as well as other related dialects)' 'have been described as having initial primary stress for all word types.. The initial syllable of the coverb receives a secondary stress' (citing Ford 1998 p. 70ff., Green 1989 p. 36, Reid 1990 p. 96). No Marri Ammu data.

sources.citation: Marett, Allan, Linda Barwick & Lysbeth Ford. 2013. For the sake of a song: Wangga songmen and their repertories. Sydney: Sydney University Press (open access, CC BY-NC-ND). Ch. 3 'The language of wangga' (Ford), Marri Tjavin-Marri Ammu section pp. 83-84; 'How to read Marri Tjavin-Marri Ammu words' pp. 16-17.
sources.note: 'Marri Ammu and Marri Tjavin share identical sound systems' (Tables 3.6-3.7: 28 consonants, 4 vowels; 98% shared cognates; Table 3.8 lexical variants). Segmental inventory only; no stress or accent statement anywhere in ch. 3 or the pronunciation guide (the only 'stressed' tokens in the book mean 'emphasised').

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1974. Daly Family Languages, Australia. Pacific Linguistics C-32. Canberra: ANU. Ch. 4b 'MareAmmu', p. 101 (also ch. 4/4a Marithiel/Marityabin pp. 70-100).
sources.note: One-page chapter: classification and seven lexical differences from Marityabin; 'The phonologies of Marityabin and MareAmmu appear to be identical.' No phoneme list for MareAmmu and no stress/accent statement; book-wide a full-text search for stress/accent gives zero hits for stress/accent/prosod (confirms the earlier scan).
